context.text: A teenager opened fire at an elementary school in Bend, Ore. , killing three children — ages 5, 8, and 11 — and a teacher, officials confirmed. A 7-year-old and a 54-year-old were hospitalized. A bystander killed the 16-year-old suspected shooter after following him into Silver Rail Elementary School, according to local officials. The suspected shooter has not been identified. Officials say he was a resident of Bend. He used a "long gun," which is similar to a rifle or shotgun, during the attack. His connection to the school — if any — remains unclear.

Today, I was proud to announce the Community Water and Energy Resource Center (CWERC) Feasibility Study, an important initiative that will explore innovative solutions to strengthen Laredo’s water supply, improve wastewater treatment, and expand renewable energy opportunities.

The proposed facility would reclaim and reuse wastewater, transform organic waste into renewable energy, and help create a more sustainable and locally controlled water resource for our community. If determined feasible, the facility could potentially recycle 2 to 3 million gallons of wastewater per day, helping reduce our dependence on the Rio Grande while meeting Laredo’s growing water needs.

This initiative is supported by $180,000 in federal funding from the North American Development Bank’s Technical Assistance Program, along with $81,500 in additional funding from RGISC, the City of Laredo, Harvard Graduate School of Design, and Zimmerman Consulting, bringing the total project investment to $261,500.

Beyond strengthening our water supply, this project could create economic opportunities, support local job creation, provide reclaimed water for businesses and irrigation, and recover valuable resources from waste. The feasibility study will evaluate the project’s engineering, environmental benefits, potential locations, and economic viability to help determine the best path forward.

I look forward to continuing our partnership with NADBank, RGISC, the City of Laredo, and our other partners to advance innovative solutions that protect our natural resources, strengthen our long-term water security, and support Laredo’s continued growth. Planning for our future means investing in sustainable solutions that will benefit our community for generations to come.

Over the summer, we learned that several servicemembers and civilians who worked at Fort Meade tragically died by suicide. One loss of life is one too many – and that is why I am committed to doing everything we can to make sure everyone at the Fort has the full mental health support and resources they need, so that a tragedy like this does not occur again. Here is an update on that work:

✔️In last year’s defense bill, I worked with colleagues to secure a provision requiring U.S. Cyber Command and the Cyber Mission Force to hire mental health professionals with security clearances at their operating locations. 

✔️I am now leading my Maryland delegation and Armed Services colleagues to help secure $11 million in funding needed to ensure full funding of this provision.

✔️I am also committed to working alongside U.S. Cyber Command to bring additional mental health resources to Fort Meade. I’m working to rectify the reporting requirements and include civilian employees in DoD’s suicide data, especially at installations like Fort Meade where civilian and uniformed officers work side by side on the same projects.

✔️Finally, I am working to address delays with the transfer of mental health licenses from out of state.
